Notice the validator is still plain TypeScript, built from the narrowing we already know. Every field starts as unknown and is checked before use.

One last step. Next, returning errors instead of throwing them.

Loading a scene can fail in three different ways: the file may be missing, it may not parse, or it may not validate. Throwing for all three forces every caller to remember a try. A Result makes failure part of the return type instead.

The errors file defines it, highlighted. A Result is a union of two shapes: ok true with a value, or ok false with errors. It is a discriminated union, the same idea as the scene nodes in Course 3, with ok as the tag. Two tiny helpers, ok and fail, build each side.

Load scene now returns a Promise of a Result of Scene or a list of strings. Inside, the read and the parse sit in a try. The catch clause declares its error as unknown, because in JavaScript anything at all can be thrown, not only Errors. So the code checks with instanceof before reading the message. Then the validator runs, and its errors become a fail.

The side pane shows what the caller gets. It must look at ok before it can touch the value, because the checker will not let it read value on the failing side. Forgetting to handle failure is no longer possible.

The main file loads three files this time, and the side pane's table lists what happened. The checkout is fixed now, so self and the checkout are both drawn. The third, shop dot json, does not exist, and instead of a crash, the terminal shows its error as a line of output: ENOENT, no such file or directory.

miniflow now reads scene files and refuses bad ones politely. Next course, it becomes a command.

miniflow has grown to a dozen files, and they have been importing each other since the model course. Before it becomes a command, it is worth looking properly at how those files connect.

Every file here is a module. Whatever a module exports, another may import, and nothing else is visible outside it. The old main file is gone. Its job moves into src slash cli dot ts, the entry point, and the highlighted lines are its imports: layout from the layout module, load scene from the loader, and the SVG renderer. The side pane draws that as the module graph: the entry point at the top, with an arrow to each module it depends on, and each of those has arrows of its own.

Two details are particular to running TypeScript directly in Node. The import paths end in dot ts, the real file names, because Node resolves exactly the path it is given. And imports of types must say so. The tsconfig gains verbatim module syntax, which makes that a rule. The scratch file imports the Scene type with a plain import, and the terminal shows the result: error TS1484. Scene is a type, and must be imported using a type-only import.

The rule exists because of erasure. An import type disappears entirely when types are stripped. A plain import stays in the JavaScript, and at run time there is no Scene to import. With the rule on, every import says honestly whether it will exist when the program runs.

The entry point runs, and writes both pictures. Next, it starts taking orders from the command line.

A command takes its instructions from the words typed after it. Node hands those over as a plain array of strings, process dot argv. Turning that into options by hand is fiddly, so Node's standard library has a parser for it, in the util module: parse args.

The highlighted call describes what the command accepts. Positional words are allowed: the subcommand and the scene's path. And there are two options. Svg is a string, the output file. Theme is a string too, with a default of dark.

What comes back is the interesting part, and the side pane's table lists what the checker knows about it. The positionals are an array of strings. Values dot svg is a string or undefined, because nobody has to pass it. Values dot theme is just a string, because it has a default, so it can never be missing. The types are worked out from the options object itself. Change an option's type, or remove its default, and every use of it is checked again.

The terminal runs the command with a subcommand, a path and an svg option, the way a user will type it. The command prints what it parsed: command render, the checkout's path, the output path, and theme dark, which nobody typed. Then it renders the scene to the file it was given.

There is a gap here, though. The command is just a string, so the code compares it with the word render and does nothing at all for anything else. Next, the command becomes a type.

miniflow will have three subcommands: render, check and watch. That is a fixed set of words, which by now we know how to type.

The highlighted line says it: Command is a union of three string literals. Below it, is command is a type guard. It takes the first positional word, which is just a string, and returns whether it is one of the three. Then the main code uses it: if the word is not a command, or there is no path, it prints the usage line to standard error and exits with a code of two, the usual code for being called wrongly.

After that guard, the checker knows the command is a Command, and the switch at the bottom routes it, as the side pane draws. Render calls the render function. Check and watch print not yet, for now. And the default branch assigns the command to never, the exhaustiveness check from the model course. If a fourth subcommand is added to the union and forgotten here, this switch stops compiling.

The terminal tries all the paths. Render on the self scene writes its picture. Check prints not yet. And a typo, draw instead of render, does not quietly do nothing. It is caught by the guard, and the usage line comes back, naming all three choices.

The same pattern works for any command-line tool: a union for the words, one guard where the text comes in, and an exhaustive switch. From the guard on, a misspelled subcommand cannot exist. Next, the check subcommand, and how a command reports failure.

Check is the subcommand a build or a CI job will run, to make sure every scene file is valid before anything is drawn. For that, it has to fail in a way a machine can see.

The highlighted function runs the loader and its validator. If the scene is fine, it prints ok, and returns zero. If not, it prints each problem with console dot error, and returns one. The switch sets the process's exit code from that number.

The side pane shows the three channels a process answers on. Standard output carries results. Standard error carries problems. And the exit code, a number the process leaves behind when it ends, says whether it succeeded: zero means yes, anything else means no.

The terminal checks two files and prints each exit code after it. The self scene prints ok, and exit zero. A deliberately broken copy, called broken dot json, prints the validator's message with its path, nodes one dot dir, expected row or column, got rows, and exit one. The third run sends standard error to dev null, which throws it away. The message disappears, but the exit code is still one. That is the point of keeping the channels apart. A script that only cares whether the scenes are valid can ignore the text completely and read the number. A person reading the terminal sees the reasons.

A command that prints an error and still exits zero is a common bug, and a nasty one: every CI job that runs it will pass. Returning the code from each handler makes the success path and the failure path equally explicit.

Next, making miniflow installable as a real command.

To be a command someone can install, a package names an executable in its package dot json: the bin field. The first attempt simply pointed the bin at src slash cli dot ts, packed the project with npm pack, and installed the tarball into a separate project called shop.

It failed, and the side pane quotes why. Node refused with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING. Node strips types from your own files, but never from files under node modules. Installed packages are expected to ship JavaScript. So for the first time in this film, tsc has to write output.

The editor shows the tsconfig that does it. No emit is gone. Root dir and out dir say where the source is and where the JavaScript goes: src in, dist out. The highlighted option, rewrite relative import extensions, solves a detail that would break everything: our imports end in dot ts, and the emitted files must import dot js. This option rewrites those paths as it emits. The allow importing TypeScript extensions option is gone, because emitting files is exactly what it forbids.

The package dot json points the bin at dist slash cli dot js, ships only the dist folder, and gains a build script that runs tsc. The terminal runs it: the build is silent, and dist holds a JavaScript file for every source file. Then the same pack and install as before. And this time npx miniflow check runs inside the shop project, and reports the self scene ok.

During development we still run the dot ts files directly. The compile step exists only for what we ship. Next, a subcommand that never finishes: watch.

Editing a scene file and running render after every change gets old quickly. Watch mode redraws a scene whenever its file is saved.

Node's file system module can watch a folder, and the promises version gives us the events in the most convenient form there is: an async iterable. The highlighted line loops over it with for await. A normal for of loop asks for the next value and gets it at once. For await asks for the next value and waits until it exists. Here, the next value is the next change to a file in the folder, so the loop body runs once per event, whenever that happens, and the loop never ends by itself.

The side pane draws the flow. Watch yields events. The loop waits for each one, prints its type and the file's name, and if the file is a JSON scene, awaits the render function from the last section, passed in as a callback.

The types flow through. Each event's file name is typed as a string or null, because some platforms do not report it, so the code checks it with optional chaining before calling ends with. And the callback's type says it takes a path and returns a promise, so watch can await it.

To record this honestly, the terminal runs watch for three seconds under the timeout command, while a script saves the self scene once in the background, exactly as an editor would. The run shows watching scenes, one change event for self dot json, and the redraw: wrote out slash self dot svg.

One save, one render. But editors do not always save that neatly. Next, many events from a few saves.

This time the background script saves the file three times in quick succession, the way a format-on-save editor or a quick double save can. The terminal shows what the watcher sees: more change events than saves, because one save can be reported more than once, and how many depends on the moment. Rendering on each would draw the same scene four times in a fraction of a second.

The fix is a classic: debounce. Wait until the events stop for a moment, then act once.

The highlighted function builds a debounced version of any function. It keeps one variable, timer, and returns a new function. Every call clears the pending timer and starts a new one. Only when two hundred milliseconds pass with no further call does the timer finally fire. The returned function closes over timer: it keeps that variable alive between calls, even though debounce itself has long since returned. That is a closure, and the side pane draws it as the box holding the pending timer.

The timer's type is worth a look. What setTimeout returns differs: in Node it is a Timeout object, and in a browser it is a number. Rather than pick one, the code says return type of typeof setTimeout: whatever this platform's setTimeout returns. Course 10 explains exactly how that type is computed. Here it simply keeps the code honest on both platforms.

Debounce is generic too, over its argument list, so the debounced function takes exactly the arguments the original did, a path here.

The run shows the burst of change events, then exactly one render. Next, stopping the watcher cleanly.

A watcher runs until someone presses Ctrl-C. By default, that kills the process wherever it happens to be. A well-behaved command stops on purpose, and cleans up on the way out.

The CLI creates an AbortController, the standard way to cancel work in JavaScript. When the process receives SIGINT, the signal Ctrl-C sends, the handler prints a line and calls abort. The controller's signal is passed into watch scenes, and from there into watch itself, highlighted. When the signal aborts, the async iterator ends by throwing an AbortError. The catch recognises that error by its name and simply returns. Anything else is still thrown.

The other highlighted line is newer JavaScript. Using declares a resource, here a small object from the announce function. It printed watching when it was created. Its dispose method, named by Symbol dot dispose, prints stopped watching. Using guarantees that dispose runs when the scope ends, however it ends: a normal return, an early return from the catch, or an exception. It is like a finally block that the resource carries with it.

The side pane follows Ctrl-C through. SIGINT arrives, abort is called, watch ends with an AbortError, the function returns, and using disposes the resource.

The terminal shows it. The watcher starts, redraws once for the background saves, and then timeout sends SIGINT after three seconds, just as Ctrl-C would. The handler prints SIGINT, stopping. And the last line is the dispose: stopped watching scenes.

miniflow is now a real command, with render, check and watch. Next course: making sure it keeps working.

miniflow works. This course is about knowing that it still works tomorrow, after the next change. The first tool is the checker itself, turned up a notch.

Strict mode, which we have used since the first course, still leaves one gap open, and it is a common one. When code reads an array by index, the checker assumes the element is there. But an index can be past the end, and then the value is undefined. The highlighted option closes the gap: no unchecked indexed access. With it on, reading an array by index gives the element type or undefined, and the code has to deal with both.

The side pane's table shows the difference on our own code. Points at i used to be a Pt. Now it is a Pt or undefined. The same goes for the spread of ports in the renderer, and the output slots in the port function.

The terminal shows what the flag found in miniflow: five places, in the route file and the SVG renderer. Two say a value has no property ta or tb, because it might be undefined. Two say a point that might be undefined cannot be destructured. One says an object is possibly undefined.

In each of these, the index happens to be safe today: the loops never step past the end. But nothing enforced that. One careless edit to a loop bound, and the first sign would have been a crash, or worse, a NaN quietly drawn into the picture. The fixes are small: a guard here, a default there.

The checker is one safety net. Next, the other one: tests.

The checker proves that the types fit together. It cannot prove that the router puts the bend in the right place. For that, we run the code on examples whose answers we know: tests.

We install Vitest, a test runner that understands TypeScript files directly, the same way Node does. The project's tsconfig now checks the test folder too, and a second config, tsconfig build, emits only the source for the bin.

The editor shows one of the route tests, highlighted. Every test has the same three steps, which the side pane names. Arrange: two rects, a hundred by forty, one beside the other with a gap. Act: call route on them. Assert: expect the result to equal exactly four points, out of the right face, to the middle of the gap, down, and into the left face. Two more tests check the faces and the port spread. The fit test checks the four percent margin and the clamp at four.

These tests are easy to write for one reason we planned for in the route course. Route and fit are pure functions. There is no setup to fake, no file to write, no clock to stop: rects in, points out, compare.

The terminal shows the install, a clean check, and then the run. Two test files, five tests, all passed, in a fraction of a second.

A test that only ever passes proves little. What counts is what it says when the code breaks. Next, we break it.

Here is a bug of the most ordinary kind. In the port function, someone tidies up the formula and drops the plus one from the bottom. Each port is now its position divided by the number of ports, instead of by one more than that. It looks almost the same. The checker has nothing to say: every number is still a number.

The test runner does. The terminal shows the whole report. One test failed: spreads three edges over one face, in order. The assertion error says the received list starts with zero point three three, where the expected one starts with zero point two five.

Then comes the most useful part, the diff, highlighted. Minus lines are what the test expected: a quarter, a half, three quarters. Plus lines are what the code returned: a third, two thirds, and one. The side pane's table lines them up. The last one is the real problem. A port at one is the very end of the face, the corner of the box, where the arrowhead would sit on the border.

Below the diff, the runner points at the line of the test that failed, with the source around it. And the summary at the bottom counts one failed and four passed.

Notice how much the test knew that the checker could not. It knew what the spread is supposed to be, because a person wrote that down when they understood it. A test is a fact about behaviour, recorded while it was right.

The plus one goes back, and the test passes again. Next, a test for the whole picture at once.

The renderer's output is several kilobytes of SVG. Writing an expected value for that by hand would be absurd. A snapshot test takes a different approach: record the output once, and from then on, compare every run with the recording.

The new test loads the checkout, draws it, and expects the SVG to match its snapshot. On the first run, there is no snapshot yet, so Vitest writes one: a file in a snapshots folder beside the test, holding the exact SVG. That run passed, and the side pane shows the stored picture on the left.

Then a change. Someone enlarges the arrowheads in the SVG document class, a marker width of eight becomes ten. It is a single attribute in one line. The terminal shows the next test run. Snapshot mismatched, and then the diff, highlighted. The minus line is the stored defs element, with a marker width of eight. The plus line is the new one, with ten. Around them, a few unchanged lines for context: the opening svg tag, the canvas rect, the first box.

A snapshot does not know whether a change is right. It only knows that something changed. So the failure is a question to the person who made it, as the note says. If the change was intended, run the tests with the update flag and the recording is replaced, and the new snapshot goes into the commit for review. If it was not intended, the test just caught a regression that no other test would have.

For a renderer, whose output is long and exact, that is the right trade. Next, testing something that only exists at compile time.

miniflow's types are part of what it offers. If someone loosened the return type of layout to any, every test would still pass, and the users of the library would quietly lose all their checking. So the types deserve tests of their own.

The new file has two kinds, highlighted. Expect type of, from Vitest, states a type. The layout function's return type must equal a Map from string to Rect, exactly. Route must return an array of points. And the literal store must extend Tone.

The other kind is a comment: ts expect error. It tells the checker the next line must fail to compile. The line under it builds an item with the tone stroe, the typo from the model course. As long as the checker refuses it, the comment is satisfied, and nothing is reported. If someone ever widened Tone to plain string, the line would compile, and the comment itself would become the error.

The scratch file shows that case. It puts the same comment over a perfectly valid item, with the tone store. The terminal shows the checker's response: error TS2578, an unused ts expect error directive. The comment promised a failure that never came.

These are tests that run in the compiler. The note says it: a type test that fails is a compile error, not a red line in the test report. The runner reports them as passing, because at run time they do almost nothing. The real verdict was given by tsc, one line earlier.

Next, a class of bug that neither the checker nor the tests saw coming.

Here is a bug that compiles, runs, and passes every test we have. In the render function, someone drops one word: the await in front of write file. The highlighted line still writes the file. Eventually.

The side pane shows the problem. Write file returns a promise. Without await, the function carries on immediately, and prints wrote, before the file has been written. Worse, if the write fails, because the disk is full or the folder is read-only, the promise rejects, and nobody is listening. The command exits zero and the error is lost. A promise that nobody awaits is called a floating promise.

tsc does not complain. Ignoring a return value is legal. The tests do not see it either, because they never call this function. A linter can, if it knows the types: it has to know that write file returns a promise, and not some other value it is fine to drop.

The usual linter for TypeScript, typescript-eslint, does not support TypeScript 7 yet. So miniflow uses oxlint, whose type-aware mode is built on TypeScript 7's own type checker. The config file turns on one rule: no floating promises, as an error.

The terminal shows the install, a clean tsc, and then the lint. Source file cli dot ts, line twenty-six, column three: promises must be awaited. And it lists the fixes: await it, handle its rejection with catch, or mark it ignored on purpose with void, which is exactly what the debounce in the command course did.

The await goes back. Next, a detour, to watch tsc itself at work.

This is a detour into the checker we have leaned on for the whole film. What does tsc actually do when we type tsc no emit? The lab asks it to report on itself, with the extended diagnostics flag, on miniflow.

The left side names its phases. The scanner reads characters and groups them into tokens: a keyword, a name, a brace. The parser turns each file's tokens into a syntax tree. The binder walks those trees and connects names to symbols: which declaration does this identifier mean, in which scope. The checker then gives every expression a type and compares it with what it must be. Emit, the phase that writes JavaScript, is skipped, because we asked for no emit.

The terminal shows the real numbers, highlighted. Files: two hundred and sixty-four. miniflow itself has about twenty, and the rest are type definitions: the JavaScript standard library, Node's types, and Vitest's. Over a hundred and thirty thousand lines in all, almost all of them declarations we never wrote. Types: about ninety-seven thousand, created on the way.

The times are the striking part. The parse, the bind and the check together took a fraction of a second, and the check is by far the largest share. That speed is what TypeScript 7 is about. The checker was rewritten in Go, compiled to native code, and runs its work in parallel. TypeScript 7 is the same language, with much the same checker, but many times faster.

Back to the project, and one command that runs every check we have.

We now have three separate tools that each catch different mistakes. Running three commands by hand, in the right order, is exactly the kind of thing people forget. So they become one.

The package dot json gains a script, highlighted: check. It runs tsc with no emit, then oxlint in type-aware mode over the source and the tests, then the test runner. The double ampersands mean each stage runs only if the one before it succeeded. And npm run check exits with the code of the stage that stopped it, so anything that runs it, a person, a git hook, a CI job, gets a single yes or no.

The side pane draws the gate. The first stage checks the types, including the strict flags and the type tests. The second catches floating promises and their kind. The third runs the behaviour: routes, ports, the fit, and the snapshot of the whole picture.

The order is deliberate, cheapest and broadest first. A type error usually means the tests would fail for a boring reason, so there is no point running them.

The terminal shows the whole gate passing. The script's name and command, a silent tsc, a silent lint, and the test run: four files, nine tests, all passed, all in well under a second.

That is what trust means here. Not that miniflow has no bugs, but that the bugs we have already met cannot come back unnoticed. From here on, this command stays green.

Next course, the types themselves become programmable.

Until now, every type in miniflow was written by hand. This course is about types that are computed from other types, and from values. It starts with a small duplication we have been carrying since the load course: the seven tone names appear twice, once in the Tone type and once in the validator's list.

The model file fixes that with one object, highlighted. Tone info maps each tone to a short description. As const freezes it, so every value keeps its exact literal type. Then the type Tone is derived from it: key of type of tone info.

Read that right to left, as the side pane does. Typeof, in a type position, means the type of this value. Key of means the union of that type's keys. So Tone is exactly the seven names, and it can never drift from the object again. The validator now uses object dot keys of the same object, so adding an eighth tone is one line in one file.

How can we see what a type turned out to be? This course uses a trick, the probe. The scratch file assigns a value of the computed type to a variable whose type is the literal word probe, which nothing can match. The checker refuses, and in refusing, it prints the type it actually has. The terminal shows both probes. The type of the store entry is the literal text keeps data. And key of type of tone info is the union of all seven names.

The check command still passes on the checkout. Next, looking up one part of a type, the way you would read a property.

A value's property is read with square brackets: item, bracket, tone. Types can be read the same way. Item, bracket, the string tone, is the type of an item's tone field, whatever that is.

The scratch file declares three of these, highlighted. The terminal probes each one. Item bracket tone comes back as the seven tones or undefined, because tone is optional. Scene node bracket type is the union of every node's tag: group, item or note. That one is interesting, because SceneNode is a union, so the lookup is done on each member and the results are joined. And the third reads two levels deep. Scene bracket nodes is the array of nodes, bracket number means the type of any element, and bracket id is that element's id: a string.

The side pane's table lists the three results.

Why bother, when we could write those types out? For the same reason as the last section: there is then nothing to keep in step. The load file shows it. Its list of node kinds is now typed as an array of scene node bracket type. If someone adds a fourth kind of node to the model, that list must include it, and the validator's error message, which joins the list, names it automatically. If someone mistypes a kind in the list, the checker refuses it.

Indexed access is how a large codebase talks about pieces of its central types without copying them. Next, building a whole new type from an existing one, key by key.

A mapped type walks over the keys of a type and builds a new property for each one. TypeScript's own Partial, which makes every field optional, is a mapped type, and the new types file writes it by hand, highlighted, as Optional.

Read the braces like a loop. For each key K in key of T, make a property called K, add a question mark to make it optional, and give it the type T bracket K, the original field's type. The side pane's table runs that loop over Item: type, id, title, sub and tone each come out with a question mark. The scratch file uses it for a patch, an object that changes only the title of an item, and the checker accepts it.

The second highlighted type goes further. Deep readonly is a mapped type that calls itself. For an array, it makes a readonly array of deep readonly elements. For any other object, it maps every key to readonly, with a deep readonly value. Anything else, a string or a number, is left as it is. That condition is a conditional type, the subject of the next section.

The point is reach. The readonly keyword from the layout course protected one level of one object. Deep readonly protects a whole scene, every node and every child of every group. The scratch file takes a deep readonly scene, finds its first group, and tries to replace its children. The terminal shows the checker refusing, with error TS2540: children is a read-only property, three levels down from where the type was applied.

Next, the question mark and colon that appeared inside that type.

A conditional type is an if for types. It reads, T extends U, question mark, one type, colon, another. If T fits U, the result is the first type, otherwise the second.

The highlighted type, Node Of, uses one to answer a useful question: given a tag, which node kind has it? Node Of group should be Group. It takes the scene node union, and for each member N, asks: does N have type K? If so, keep N. If not, never.

The words for each member matter. When a conditional type is applied to a union, it runs once per member, and the results are joined. That is called distribution, and the side pane draws it for Node Of group. Item is asked and gives never. Group is asked and is kept. Note gives never. And never disappears from a union, so what is left is just Group.

The terminal probes three uses. Node Of group is Group. Node Of item or note comes back as Item, then Note: two kinds kept, one dropped. And the third probe asks for Node Of edge, a tag no node has. There is no error at all for that line. Every member gave never, and never, the empty type, can be assigned to anything, even to the word probe. A silent probe is the answer.

TypeScript's built-in Extract is this same pattern. Writing it once by hand is what makes the built-ins readable rather than magic.

Next, a conditional type that does more than test a shape: it takes a piece of it.

A conditional type can test whether a type has a shape. With infer, it can also capture part of that shape, the way a pattern match pulls a value out of a structure.

The first highlighted type is Element Of. It asks whether T is an array of something, and the word infer E names that something. If T is an array, the answer is E, the element type. If not, never. The second is Return Of, our own version of TypeScript's ReturnType, which the debounce in the command course used. It asks whether F is a function, whatever its arguments, returning something it calls R. If so, the answer is R.

The side pane shows the idea: match the shape, capture the hole.

The terminal probes three uses. Element Of scene bracket nodes is SceneNode. Return Of type of layout is a Map from string to Rect: the checker read the layout function's own declaration and pulled out its return type. And the third combines them. Return Of type of route is an array of points, so Element Of that is one point, Pt, the tuple from the route course.

This is how types are derived from functions without ever writing them again. A test can say: whatever layout returns, this helper takes the same thing. If layout's return type changes, everything derived from it changes too, and the checker re-checks every use. Return type of set timeout, from the command course, worked exactly like this.

Next, a type that is the same as a string at run time, and different at compile time.

Node ids and labels are both strings, and that is a problem. A function that expects an id will happily take a label, or a title, or any text at all. A branded type gives an id its own type, without changing it at run time.

The highlighted type, NodeId, is a string intersected with an object that has a brand field. No real string has that field, so no plain string is a NodeId. But nothing exists at run time either: the brand is never created. A NodeId is an ordinary string with a different name in the checker.

The only way to make one is the function below it. Node id takes a string and the set of known ids, checks the string is among them, and only then returns it as a NodeId. That as is the one claim in the whole scheme, and it sits right behind a real check.

The side pane follows a string through. Api is just a string. Node id checks it, and what comes out is a NodeId, which the checker now trusts.

The scratch file has a map of rects keyed by NodeId. Looking up node id of api is fine. The terminal shows the two that are not. Looking up the plain string api is refused, and so is looking up a label, paid. Both give error TS2345: a string is not assignable to NodeId, because it lacks the brand.

The cost is one function call wherever text becomes an id. The gain is that the checker can tell an id from any other string, everywhere it travels. Next, a type that describes the text itself.

Some strings have a grammar. An edge could aim at one face of a box, written as an address: the node's id, a dot, and the face, as in api dot right. Template literal types can describe that grammar exactly.

The highlighted type, Port, is written with backticks, like a template string, but with types in the holes. Any string, then a dot, then a Side, the union of left, right, top and bottom from the route course. The side pane draws the three parts. Because Side is a union, Port is really four patterns: anything ending in dot left, dot right, dot top, or dot bottom.

Below it, parse port splits an address into its id and its side. The return type is a labelled tuple again. The cast on the side is safe, because the input's type has already guaranteed what follows the dot.

The scratch file tries some addresses, and the side pane's table lists the results. Api dot right is a Port. Api dot rigth, with the letters swapped, is refused with error TS2322, and the message lists all four patterns it failed to match. Plain api, with no face at all, is refused too.

The scratch file also runs, and parse port splits two good addresses into their parts: api and right, orders and left.

So the checker now validates the inside of a string, a thing that in most languages needs a regular expression at run time.

One step left: using all of this to catch the paymnet typo before anything runs.

In the route course, a typo in an edge, paymnet instead of payments, got all the way to run time before a SceneError caught it. This section moves that catch to compile time, using what this course built.

The checkout scene is written in code again, through a new helper called define scene, and the highlighted line is the typo, back on purpose.

Define scene has a type parameter N for the nodes, and it is marked const. That is a newer TypeScript feature. Normally, an object literal passed to a function is widened: the id api becomes just string. A const type parameter keeps everything exactly as written, as if the caller had added as const. So N holds every node with its literal id.

A type called ids of then walks N, with a conditional type and infer, collecting each node's id, and recursing into each group's children. The side pane draws the flow: the literal nodes, into ids of, giving a union of twelve ids. The edges parameter then requires every from and every to to be one of those twelve.

The terminal shows the result. One error, at line forty-two of the scene file, exactly on the typo: error TS2322, the type paymnet is not assignable to the type api, or browser, or cart, and so on, all twelve ids listed. The editor would underline it as it was typed.

That is the payoff of type-level programming. The scene's own data became the type that checks it. With the typo fixed, npm run check is green again.

Next course, miniflow runs in a browser.

Everything miniflow has drawn so far was a file, written by Node. This course draws the scene live, in a web page, and the page will teach us something about why the engine works the way it does.

A browser cannot run TypeScript, and does not understand imports that end in dot ts. Something has to sit between our source and the browser. That is Vite, a development server. We install it, pinned like everything else.

The new web folder holds the page. The editor shows index dot html: a header, an empty main element where the scene will go, and one script tag, highlighted, that loads main dot ts as a module. For now, main dot ts only sets the page's title and logs a line, to prove the page runs.

The side pane follows a request. The browser asks for the page, and Vite serves the HTML. The page asks for main dot ts, and Vite strips its types, the same way Node does, and serves JavaScript. Each import main makes is another request, answered the same way, so the browser loads the module graph one file at a time, exactly as we wrote it. Nothing is bundled while we develop, which is why it starts so fast.

The terminal starts Vite on the web folder, under the timeout command so the recording ends. Vite prints its version, ready in a fraction of a second, and the local address: localhost, port fifty-one seventy-three. The tsc check before it is silent, because the web folder is now part of the project the checker covers.

Next, the types that describe a page.

In a page, code talks to the DOM, the tree of elements the browser built from the HTML. TypeScript ships types for all of it, and they are honest in one way that surprises people at first.

The highlighted lines find the main element by its id with query selector, and set its text. The terminal shows the checker refusing the second line: error TS18047, host is possibly null.

The side pane's table explains why. Query selector searches the page for a selector, and nothing guarantees a match. The HTML might change, or the id might be mistyped. When nothing matches, it returns null. So its type is an element or null, and the checker will not let us use the result until we have dealt with the null.

The table also shows how precise these types are. The scratch probe asks for query selector of the word main, a tag name, and the terminal prints its type: HTMLElement or null, because for a known tag name the library knows exactly what kind of element it is. For an id like scene, it can only say Element. And for the theme button we will add later, a type argument says what we expect: an HTMLButtonElement or null.

The fix is the narrowing from the model course, applied to the page. Check for null once, near the top, and throw a clear error if the element is missing. After that check, the checker knows host is an element on every line below.

This is the browser's version of the lesson from the loading course: a value from outside the program, here the page, starts unchecked. Next, the scene goes into the page.

Drawing the scene in the page takes very little new code, and that is the point of this section.

The import at the top of the file brings the checkout scene in as a JSON module, with an import attribute saying its type is json. The scene file does not change. Then, highlighted, assert scene checks it, the same validator that guards the command line, and the renderer draws it. The last line puts the SVG string into the main element with inner HTML.

One thing did have to move, and the side pane shows why. The validator used to live in the load file, next to read file from Node's file system module. A page has no file system, and importing that module would break the page. So the validator moves to its own file, validate dot ts, which imports nothing from Node, and the load file re-exports it, so every existing import keeps working. The terminal confirms that: the check is silent, and all nine tests still pass after the move.

The renderer did not change by a single line. It never knew it was writing a file. It only ever built a string, and a string is as useful to a page as to a disk.

The bottom panel is the live page, from the step's own Vite server, shown at the URL localhost, port fifty-one seventy-three. The checkout is there, exactly as the SVG file looked in the route course: the same boxes, the same arrows, the same monospace text.

But a web page can use any font. Next, we let it.

Since the layout course, every box has been sized by counting characters: nine point six pixels each, which is only true for a monospace font. A page can draw any font, and in a proportional font an i is much narrower than an m. Counting characters would make every box the wrong width.

The fix is to ask the browser. But the layout runs in Node too, and Node has no fonts to ask. So the layout must not know how text is measured. It should be told.

The editor shows how, highlighted. Measurer is an interface with one method: give it a line of text, and it returns its width. Mono is the old rule, wrapped as a Measurer. Layout now takes a measurer as a parameter, with mono as the default, and passes it down to every size calculation. Nothing in the layout file knows which one it has. That is dependency injection: a function receives what it depends on, rather than reaching out for it.

The side pane draws the two implementations behind one interface. Mono for Node and the command line. And in the page, a canvas measurer: it asks a canvas element to measure text in the page's real font, sans serif here, with measure text. The SVG renderer takes the font name too, so the boxes and the text agree.

The bottom panel shows the difference. The same checkout, now in a proportional font. Every box fits its own words, and most are narrower than before, because most letters are narrower than a monospace cell. The layout moved, and the arrows followed, because they are routed from the rects.

The tests still pass, untouched, because they use the default. Next, the page responds to a click.

The palette from the draw course has a dark theme and a light one. The page gets a button to switch between them, and with it, events.

The header gains a button with the id theme. The main file finds it with query selector, passing HTMLButtonElement as a type argument, and checks both elements for null in one go. A variable holds the current theme, typed as Theme, so it can only ever be dark or light.

Draw is now a function. It renders the scene with the current theme, sets the theme on the page's body so the background follows, and labels the button with the theme a click would switch to. Notice the scene itself: after the assertion, it is captured in a constant. Inside a function, the checker cannot assume a narrowing done outside it still holds, so the narrowed value is kept in a const that cannot change.

The highlighted line is the event. Add event listener names the event, click, and passes a handler. The handler's parameter is a MouseEvent, and the event name is what tells the checker that. Listen for a key press instead, and the parameter would be a KeyboardEvent. The DOM types keep a map from every event name to its event type, and add event listener looks the name up in it with key of and an indexed access type, both from Course 10.

The side pane follows one click. The browser makes a MouseEvent, the handler flips the theme and logs where the click happened, and draw renders the same rects with the other palette. The layout is not run again, because nothing about the sizes changed.

The bottom panel shows the page after a click, in the light theme. Next, filling the window.

A diagram on a page should fill the space it has, and keep filling it when the window changes size. The function for that already exists. We wrote it in the layout course and tested it in the trust course: fit.

The new place function, highlighted, finds the SVG in the page and reads its natural size. It reads the size of the main element, the frame it must fit. Then fit returns a scale and an offset, exactly as it did in Node, with the same four percent margin. Place applies them as a CSS transform: translate by the offset, then scale. A transform only changes how the element is drawn. Nothing is laid out again, so it is cheap to do often.

And it does need doing often. Near the end of the file, one line creates a ResizeObserver, a browser API that calls a function whenever an element changes size. It watches the main element, so when the window is resized, place runs again and the diagram is fitted to the new size. Draw calls place too, after every theme change.

The side pane follows that chain: the observer, the pure fit function, the transform.

It is worth noticing how little of this is new. The fit math was written once, as a pure function from sizes to a transform, with no idea where it would be used. It ran in a lab in Course 4, under tests in Course 9, and now in a browser, unchanged. That is what pure functions buy.

The bottom panel shows the result in the light theme: the checkout scaled up to fill the page, centred, every box larger and easier to read. Next, building the page for real.

During development, Vite serves every module separately, as written. That is fast to start and easy to debug, but a real site should not make one request per source file. For production, Vite builds the page into a few optimised files.

The terminal runs vite build on the web folder. It transforms fifteen modules: the page's own main file, and every module of miniflow it imports, the layout, the router, the renderer, the palette, the validator. Then it writes the result into a dist folder inside web, and reports each file's size, before and after gzip compression.

The side pane's table lists them. The HTML page is well under one kilobyte. The stylesheet is under half a kilobyte. And the whole of miniflow, the engine we have built over ten courses, comes to about ten kilobytes of JavaScript, and under four and a half once compressed. No framework, no runtime dependencies: just our code.

Two things happened to that code on the way. Every type was erased, as always. And the modules were bundled into a single file, minified, with names shortened and whitespace removed.

Look at the file names too. Each has a hash in it, a short code computed from the file's contents. If the contents change, the name changes. So a browser can keep a copy of a file forever, and a new release is always fetched fresh. The note says exactly that.

The engine now runs in two worlds: a command in Node, and a page in a browser, from the same source. One step remains: letting other people install it. That is the last course.

miniflow works as a command and as a page. The last course makes it a library other people can install. That starts with a decision: what may they import?

The new index file is the answer, the public surface. It re-exports a chosen few things, and the highlighted lines are the heart of it: layout and the measurer, the SVG renderer, and define scene. Alongside them come the model's types, fit, the validator and SceneError. Everything else stays inside.

The side pane draws the line. Above it, what is exported, and every export is a promise. Once someone builds on layout's signature, changing it breaks their code. Below it, the router, the port spread, the SVG document class, the outline renderer, the command line and the watcher. They are free to change in any release, because nobody outside can reach them.

Notice what is not exported: load scene. It reads files with Node's file system module, and exporting it would make the whole package unusable in a browser. The browser course already showed which parts of miniflow are portable, and the surface keeps only those.

The terminal shows the surface from the outside. tsc is silent. Then Node imports the index file and lists its keys. There are nine, and every one is a value: SceneError, the renderer, the tone info, the validators, define scene, fit, layout and mono. The types are exports too, but none of them appears in that list, because at run time they do not exist. They exist for tsc only, and getting them to a user's tsc is the next section.

A user's project will install miniflow's compiled JavaScript, which has no types left in it. For their checker to know miniflow's types, the package ships declaration files: one dot d dot ts beside each dot js, holding only the types.

The build config gains two options, highlighted. Declaration tells tsc to write them. Isolated declarations adds a rule, and the side pane quotes what it found on the first build: error TS9010, in the palette file, a variable must have an explicit type annotation. The palette's type had been inferred through satisfies, and inferring it needs the whole program. Isolated declarations insists that every exported value's type can be read from its own file alone, so that tools faster than tsc can produce declarations file by file. The fix was one annotation: the palette is a record of theme to theme colours.

The terminal shows the build passing, and fifteen declaration files in dist. Then one of them, fit dot d dot ts, printed whole. It is the source with the code removed: the Transform interface exactly as written, and the fit function reduced to its signature, with declare in front. Nothing in it would run. Everything in it is what a user's editor will show when they hover over fit.

The side pane draws who reads which file. Node reads the JavaScript and never looks at the declarations. tsc reads the declarations and never needs the JavaScript.

For libraries written in plain JavaScript, people write declaration files by hand, and TypeScript even lets a project describe an untyped module with declare module. Here, tsc writes them all. Next, telling npm which files to ship.

The package dot json now describes a library, not just a project. Two fields matter most.

Exports maps import paths to files. A user writes import from miniflow, nothing more, and the side pane follows that path. The dot entry says that for types, tsc should read dist slash index dot d dot ts, and for imports, Node should load dist slash index dot js. Anything not listed in exports cannot be imported at all, which enforces the public surface from the last section at the package level: nobody can reach into dist and import the router directly.

Files lists what goes into the tarball: only dist. Not the source, not the tests, not the scenes or the web page. A prepack script runs the build first, so a packed tarball can never contain stale JavaScript.

The terminal shows npm pack with dry run, which lists what would be packed without writing anything. The tarball contents are every compiled file: a dot js and a dot d dot ts for each source file, highlighted where the index pair appears, and the package dot json. Then the details: the name and version, one point oh point oh, a package size of about ten kilobytes, and thirty-seven files in total.

Reading that list before every release is a good habit. It is the only place that shows exactly what users will receive, and it catches the classics: a forgotten build, a secret file, or a test fixture of several megabytes.

The list looks right. But a list is not proof that it works. Next, installing it somewhere else.

Before publishing a package, install it the way a stranger would. Not from the source folder, where everything happens to be in reach, but from the tarball, into a project that has never seen miniflow.

That project is examples slash shop, a tiny folder with its own package dot json and tsconfig. Its main file, in the editor, is what a user would write. The highlighted line imports the renderer, define scene, layout, and the Item type, all from the bare name miniflow. Below it, one node is written as an Item, and two more inside define scene, with two edges. Then it draws the scene and writes shop dot svg.

The side pane follows the test. The terminal packs the real tarball, then installs it into the shop project, together with TypeScript and Node's types, exactly as a new user would. Then the two checks that matter. tsc, in the shop project, is silent: it found miniflow's declaration files through the exports map, and every import, every type, and the compile-time edge check of define scene all work from the installed package. And node runs main dot ts, and prints shop dot svg drawn with miniflow.

This test catches problems that no test inside the repository can. A file missing from the files list. An exports path with a typo. A declaration that refers to a type that was never emitted. Each of these passes every check in miniflow's own project, because there, the source is right next door.

Our first release is ready. Next, the hardest part of maintaining a library: changing it.

Months pass, and someone decides the field called sub should be called subtitle. It reads better. The highlighted line in the model makes the change, and the rename is carried through the layout, the renderers, the validator, and every scene file.

The terminal's first line shows that, as far as miniflow itself is concerned, everything is fine. The whole check passes: types, lint, and every test, including the snapshot, because the picture did not change. Inside the repository, this is a safe refactor.

But for users, it breaks things. The terminal bumps the version with npm version major, to two point oh point oh, packs it, and installs it into the shop project. Then tsc in the shop project fails, at the line with the Item, with error TS2353: sub does not exist in type Item. A user who upgraded would see exactly this.

That is what the version number is for, and the side pane's table states the promise of semantic versioning. A patch, the last number, is a fix: nothing a user relies on changes. A minor, the middle number, adds something new and breaks nothing. A major, the first number, is allowed to break things, and must be used whenever it does. Renaming a public field is a major, so this is two point oh point oh.

Notice who noticed. Not miniflow's own tests, which all passed. The consumer did. Keeping a small consumer like the shop project, and checking it on every release, is how a library learns that it is about to break someone.

Last section: the shop catches up, and what comes next.

The shop project upgrades to version two. The highlighted line is the only change it needs: sub becomes subtitle, as the error said. The terminal shows tsc silent again, and node drawing the scene with miniflow two point oh point oh.

The bottom panel is the picture it drew: a web shop, an API and a Postgres database, with arrows between them. The library we started building from a single box in Course 2 is now installed, typed and drawing in someone else's project.

Look at what that box became. A model of typed data, with unions and narrowing that make a forgotten case a compile error. A layout built from recursion, generics and generators. A renderer behind an interface. A router of pure functions. A loader that trusts nothing it reads. A command, a page, tests and a linter. Types that compute, and catch a typo in an edge before it runs. And a package, with declarations and a version number that means something.

The side pane points to what comes next. miniflow returns a string of SVG, which a web page can show in many ways. The sequel to this film wraps it in a React component, a Scene, that takes a scene as a property and redraws when it changes. graphl-flow, the larger engine that drew every frame of this film, is exactly that kind of component, and the next film builds one.

That is miniflow, built from one box to a shipped package.
